originalTitle: Labor women outnumber men in the caucus. Why are they overlooked as Albanese’s potential successor?
summary: Kate Ellis now heads an all-female executive as women hold a majority in the party room for the first time. But when talk turns to leadership, women barely rate
content: On Thursday, Kate Ellis was elevated to become Labor’s national president, leading for the first time an all-female team at the top of the party’s organisational wing, with two female vice-presidents. The former Rudd and Gillard government minister joins the Australian Council of Trade Unions president, Sally McManus, and its secretary, Michele O’Neill, as some of the most powerful members of the labour movement. But as the federal caucus, again for the first time, has more women than men, they barely get a mention in discussions about who will succeed Anthony Albanese. ‘Everyone wants to talk to her’ This term, Tanya Plibersek will become the longest serving woman of the House of Representatives in Australia. Plibersek has held senior cabinet and shadow cabinet roles since 2004, was deputy leader to Bill Shorten between 2013 and 2019 and is one of the most recognisable politicians in the country. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email One Labor MP, speaking anonymously, said: “The public love her, you’ve only got to walk down the street with her, and everyone wants to shake her hand, everyone wants to talk to her.” But in the conversation of who is in line to be Labor’s next leader after Albanese, Plibersek barely registers, nor do any other women. And for a party that has taken enormous pride in achieving gender parity in its caucus – where women now make up a majority of the party room and cabinet – the leadership pipeline is almost entirely fielded by men. In conversations with more than a dozen MPs, staffers and former parliamentarians, one name came up most as the successor to Albanese: the health and NDIS minister, Mark Butler. In public polls and news articles, Jim Chalmers is also mentioned, as is the deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, and minister for home affairs, Tony Burke. If a leadership ballot was called tomorrow, many believe Plibersek would not have the votes among the left faction, let alone the entire caucus. Butler is the most senior member of the faction, and resides in Albanese’s innermost circle, unlike Plibersek, whose relationship with the prime minister fell out after she backed Shorten in 2013. The move also turned some of the left faction away from her, according to one Labor source. Pamela Anderson, the chief executive of Emily’s List, which promotes gender equity within Labor, said there was certainly an “optics” problem with both the prime minister and his deputy being men. “They’re [Albanese and Marles] doing really good work around encouraging and making space for women, but it would just be, I think, fantastic to have [a woman in] one of those positions.” Veteran activist Sheila O’Sullivan, who was instrumental in Labor establishing gender quotas that 35% of candidates in winnable seats had to be women by 2002, said Albanese had “extraordinary control” of his cabinet and caucus. “He’s always been a master at assembling support and in negotiating agreements so his leadership is really very significant,” O’Sullivan said. “For [Plibersek], the issue goes back to when Shorten offered her the job as his deputy … and if you do that, then you know, by definition you wear the consequences of what do the other left members think.” But several MPs past and present said they “wouldn’t put it past Tanya” to have another go at the leadership, even if she would struggle without control in the caucus. The power brokers are still blokes Several Labor sources said part of the reason why there were so few women – if any – in contention was because “the power brokers are still very much blokes”. Butler is the most senior member of the party’s left faction, other than Albanese, while Burke and the energy minister, Chris Bowen, head two sub-factions of the NSW right, Marles leads the Victorian right, Chalmers has the Queensland right, and Don Farrell, the special minister of state, leads the right in the “small states”: South Australia, Tasmania and the Northern Territory. Just two women – Penny Wong in South Australia and the Senate president, Sue Lines, in WA – lead their left factions. One Labor MP said the situation would remain while men were in charge. “We have really impressive women, but why aren’t they seen as contenders? The challenge for women in cabinet is also that they are constrained by this kind of command and control culture.” Another Labor source noted that women often face the brunt of bad media or difficult decisions. They pointed to when Plibersek and Albanese had that awkward moment at the 2025 Labor campaign launch when she went in for a hug, he refused, and it turned into an elbow bump. The story went on in the media for days, but it would have quickly “blown over” if that had been a bloke, the source claimed. They added that women were more risk-averse, and would face stronger pushback both internally from Albanese and from the public if they started getting more leadership attention. Anderson said toxic social media was a significant issue, and added some women in the party also feared being treated the way Julia Gillard was as prime minister. “They’re 100% worried about those attacks. They are always violent [threats] and always very personal. They’re about physical assault, not just you, but your family members as well. They’ll bring people’s children into it … and the more senior you are, the more violent and more vicious those attacks are.” Wong and the finance minister, Katy Gallagher, are two of the most senior and powerful women in government – though both are in the Senate and have no intention of moving to the house, which would be necessary to become leader. A Labor source claimed their position in the Senate meant they were not seen as a “threat” by Albanese or other senior factional leaders. “The PM has a good relationship with Katy and Wong because they’re not a threat and they don’t pretend to be,” they said. chineseTitle: 核心小组中工党女性人数超过男性。为什么他们被忽视为阿尔巴内塞的潜在继任者？
chineseSummary: 凯特·埃利斯 (Kate Ellis) 现在领导着一位全女性高管，这是女性首次在聚会场所占据多数。但当话题转向领导力时，女性几乎不评价
chineseContent: 周四，凯特·埃利斯被提升为工党全国主席，首次领导该党组织高层的全女性团队，并有两名女性副总统。这位前陆克文和吉拉德政府部长与澳大利亚工会理事会主席莎莉·麦克马纳斯及其秘书米歇尔·奥尼尔一起，成为劳工运动中最有权势的成员之一。但由于联邦核心小组中女性人数首次多于男性，因此在讨论谁将接替安东尼·阿尔巴内塞的讨论中，她们几乎没有被提及。 “每个人都想和她说话” 这个任期，塔尼娅·普利伯塞克将成为澳大利亚众议院任职时间最长的女性。普利伯塞克自 2004 年以来一直担任高级内阁和影子内阁职务，并在 2013 年至 2019 年期间担任比尔·肖顿 (Bill Shorten) 的副领导人，是该国最知名的政治家之一。一位匿名工党议员表示：“公众爱她，你只要和她一起走在街上，每个人都想与她握手，每个人都想与她交谈。”但在讨论谁将成为阿尔巴内斯之后的工党下一任领导人时，普利伯塞克几乎没有参与其中，其他女性也没有。对于一个为在核心小组中实现性别平等而感到无比自豪的政党——现在女性在党室和内阁中占大多数——领导层几乎完全由男性担任。在与十几位国会议员、工作人员和前议员的谈话中，阿尔巴内塞的继任者中出现最多的一个名字是：卫生部长和全国残疾保险（NDIS）部长马克·巴特勒（Mark Butler）。在公共民意调查和新闻文章中，还提到了吉姆·查默斯、副总理理查德·马勒斯和外交部长。
whyItMatters: 这条信息属于全球新闻信号，适合用于观察外部环境、政策变化、地缘风险和市场情绪。
